analysis.one_liner: Requires carmakers to publicly disclose more defect data, especially for fatal incidents.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in the final weeks of 2014, referred to committee, and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require car and parts makers to hand over extra documents when a vehicle defect causes a death — including the claims that first notified the manufacturer and any police reports — and enter them into a public federal safety database. It would also make that database easier to search and require public online notice of all federal vehicle-safety inspections and investigations.
analysis.who_benefits: Car buyers and anyone hurt by a vehicle defect. They would get searchable public access to defect reports, fatality data, and government safety investigations, making it easier to spot dangerous patterns before a recall.

how_it_helps.text: When a reported defect incident involves a fatality, manufacturers must submit the initial claims documents, police or accident-reconstruction reports, and any amendments to the federal safety regulator.

That fatality-related information must be publicly disclosed and entered into the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration's early warning database, searchable by manufacturer, make, model, year, and defect type.

The bill directs regulators to presume in favor of maximum public availability and says trade-secret confidentiality rules cannot be used to block disclosure of production figures, death and injury incidents, property damage claim counts, and aggregated consumer complaints.

It requires the agency to overhaul its public safety databases so consumers can search, sort, and download defect information across databases at once, and to post public notice of every inspection and investigation online immediately.

analysis.who_pays: Motor vehicle and parts manufacturers, who would bear the cost of compiling and surrendering more detailed incident documents and would lose some ability to keep defect-related data confidential.

drawbacks.text: Compiling additional claims documents, police reports, and accident reconstructions for every fatal incident adds compliance costs for vehicle manufacturers.

Publishing raw, uncorroborated claims and initial incident reports before they are verified could put incomplete or disputed information about crashes into the public record, and may raise privacy concerns for people involved in the underlying claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real but modest: more transparent defect data helps consumers identify dangerous vehicles sooner. The costs fall almost entirely on manufacturers in the form of reporting burdens and lost confidentiality, and the transparency provisions are not controversial on their merits. The main weakness is that the bill arrived at the very end of a Congress, giving it essentially no chance to be considered.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in December 2014, and the Congress ended three weeks later without any committee action or floor vote.

narrative.text: Representative Matt Cartwright introduced the bill with Representative Nolan as an original cosponsor on December 11, 2014, less than a month before the 113th Congress ended.
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it.
The bill carried one cosponsor in total, and no committee markup, hearing, or floor vote occurred before the Congress expired on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Vehicle manufacturers are better off: defect reports, fatality data, and investigation records remain as confidential as they were before, and the expanded public database was never built. Consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Matt Cartwright
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill in the House and secured its referral to the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: Rep. Rick Nolan
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, making it the bill's only cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; it never reached a markup or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, but there were no votes, so no party split was ever measured.

industries.note: The bill would require makers to surrender detailed documents on fatal defect incidents and would strip trade-secret protections from production figures, death and injury data, and complaint counts. Their interest in keeping that data confidential runs directly against consumers' ability to identify dangerous vehicles. Automakers were not recorded as acting on the bill, which died in committee before any organized opposition surfaced.
